definitions.text: To inclose or fortify as with a wall. Spenser.
An inner wall; specifically (Metal.), the inner wall, or lining, of a blast furnace.
Being or placed within; inner; interior; -- opposed to outward. Milton.
Seated in the mind, heart, spirit, or soul. "Inward beauty." Shak.
Intimate; domestic; private. [Obs.] All my inward friends abhorred me. Job xix. 19. He had had occasion, by one very inward with him, to know in part the discourse of his life. Sir P. Sidney.
That which is inward or within; especially, in the plural, the inner parts or organs of the body; the viscera. Jer. Taylor. Then sacrificing, laid the inwards and their fat. Milton.
The mental faculties; -- usually pl. [Obs.]
An intimate or familiar friend or acquaintance. [Obs.] "I was an inward of his." Shak.
Toward the inside; toward the center or interior; as, to bend a thing inward.
Into, or toward, the mind or thoughts; inwardly; as, to turn the attention inward. So much the rather, thou Celestial Light, Shine inward. Milton.
In the inner parts; internally. Let Benedick, like covered fire, Consume away in sighs, waste inwardly. Shak.
Toward the center; inward; as, to curve inwardly.
In the heart or mind; mentally; privately; secretas, he inwardly repines.
Intimately; thoroughly. [Obs.] I shall desire to know him more inwardly. Beau. & Fl.
Internal or true state; essential nature; as, the inwardness of conduct. Sense can not arrive to the inwardness Of things. Dr. H. More.
Intimacy; familiarity. [Obs.] Shak.
Heartiness; earnestness. What was wanted was more inwardness, more feeling. M. Arnold.
See Inward.
To weave in or together; to intermix or intertwine by weaving; to interlace. Down they cast Their crowns, inwove with amaranth and gold. Milton.
To encircle. [R.] Beau. & Fl.
Inward sense; mind; understanding; conscience. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Within. [Obs.] This purse hath she inwith her bosom hid. Chaucer.
To work in or within.
Worn, wrought, or stamped in. [R.] Milton.
To cover by wrapping; to involve; to infold; as, to inwrap in a cloak, in smoke, etc.
To involve, as in difficulty or perplexity; to perplex. [R.] Bp. Hall.
To surround or encompass as with a wreath. [Written also enwreathe.] Resplendent locks, inwreathed with beams. Milton.

Wrought or worked in or among other things; worked into any fabric so as to from a part of its texture; wrought or adorned, as with figures. His mantle hairy, and his bonnet sedge, Inwrought with figures dim. Milton.
